source.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
source.authors: Aryaman Arora; Zheng-Xuan Wu; Jacob Steinhardt; Sarah Schwettmann

record.file_problem: none; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses whether neuron-basis representations can be useful and interpretable, and reports neuron-level circuit and steering results. It does not measure polysemanticity or test whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs, whether those mixtures share a used feature, or how common such neurons are.
record.gate_note: The circuit-sparsity comparisons and attribution patterns concern circuit tracing, not rates of polysemantic neurons. The steering results show causal roles for selected neurons or groups, but do not assess whether their responses mix unrelated inputs.
record.test_reason: The paper compares circuit sparsity and faithfulness of MLP neurons against SAE features, and steers selected neurons in case studies. It never measures how many neurons respond to unrelated inputs. It also does not test what causes mixed responses or how measurement choices affect polysemanticity. It discusses neuron interpretability only in passing.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that neuron-level circuit tracing on MLP activations (with RelP attribution) matches SAE circuits at equivalent sparsity. They add that neuron circuits reproduce CLT case-study findings and give new user-modelling results. They frame this as a challenge to the belief that neuron bases are uninterpretable, but do not measure polysemanticity.
record.recipe_differences: The study's circuit-tracing and steering methods are not a reproduction of the original vision-neuron methods or the cited SoLU work.
record.method_sensitivity: The single-neuron steering experiment varies the steering multiplier from 0 to 2; Figure 6 shows selected steering multipliers for cluster interventions.

fits_no_version.finding: MLP-activation neuron circuits in Llama 3.1 8B and Gemma-2 reach SAE-level sparsity and faithfulness on SVA (≈100-200 neurons with RelP). Selected neurons steer state-capital outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Circuits traced in the pre-down-projection MLP neuron basis are about as sparse and faithful as SAE-feature circuits.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306 (2026)
record.problems: The study does not systematically assess polysemanticity. The relevant case studies are selected tasks and neurons; the authors also manually exclude 12 neurons from the traced circuits.
record.rows_left_out: Circuit-size, faithfulness, completeness, attribution-method, and feature-scoring results were left out because they measure circuit tracing or task-feature attribution rather than polysemanticity or unrelated input responses.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons and no layer comparison. Neuron descriptions in Tables 5 and 7 (e.g. mod-10 neurons described as dates or years) are shown, but mixed selectivity is not quantified.
Superposition is not tested as a cause.
The authors speculate that gated MLPs and MoE favour sparsity, but no polysemanticity rate is compared across architectures.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not re-examined.
No test of activation range or explanation scoring.

record.verdict_notes: The appendix tables list neuron auto-descriptions that often appear unrelated to the neuron's task role. For example, mod-10 neurons are described as date or year neurons. This is anecdotal and unquantified, so it is not counted as evidence on V2 or V6.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test mixed responses in image-classifier neurons.
Does not estimate the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare such shares across layers.
Does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by superposition or capacity pressure.
Does not test polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.
Compares circuit-tracing representations across models, but does not test how architecture, activation function, or regularization changes the share of polysemantic neurons.
Does not examine canonical polysemantic neurons to determine whether their mixed responses share a coherent feature.
Does not test how the measured prevalence of polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation scoring.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Steered the Texas-example circuit clusters by multiplying their original activations; the text summarizes the result across clusters.
rows.measure: Change in the model's top prediction
rows.value: All clusters except the state cluster changed the top prediction; changes corresponded to the hypothesized cluster roles.
rows.note: The authors also say suppressing the Texas cluster leads the model to output capitals of other states. This is evidence about causal roles of selected neurons, not about polysemanticity.
rows.check: Cluster steering on one hand-selected Texas example shows causal roles, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Baseline is the unsteered output in Figure 6 (Austin 96.88%). 'Observed' concerns steering efficacy, not any version.

rows.subject: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct
rows.operation_detail: Steered neuron L23/N8079- by scaling its original activation.
rows.measure: Output probabilities for the capital, state, and original city; whether the top output flips
rows.baseline: The unsteered model's output probabilities are plotted in Figure 7; exact baseline values not stated in the text.
rows.value: The neuron can flip the top output from the capital to the state in a majority of examples.
rows.note: The probability curves are shown in Figure 7; the text gives the majority-of-examples outcome. This demonstrates a selected neuron's causal role, not whether its inputs are polysemantic.
rows.check: Single-neuron steering across 50 prompts measures causal effect on output probabilities, not polysemanticity.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
